sources.title: Slav Defense: Exchange Variation (1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.cxd5 cxd5), annotated study
Exchange Slav; search summary (Chessable, Semi-Slav Wikipedia, Exeter Chess Club, TheChessWorld; snippet only)

overview: White captures on d5 and Black recaptures with the c-pawn, giving a symmetrical pawn structure (d4 against d5) with the c-file open to both sides. Both players develop quickly and rooks often come to the c-file, where a trade is common. White tries for a small edge with the extra tempo, usually with 4.Nc3 Nf6 5.Bf4 (or 4.Bf4 first to stop ...e5) and a later Qb3 hitting b7. Black develops the light-squared bishop with ...Bf5 before ...e6, and answers Qb3 with ...Na5, then plays ...e6 and ...Bd6 or ...a5/...b5 queenside expansion. The reputation is drawish and static ('the system that takes the fun out of playing the Slav'), and it is used by top players as a drawing weapon, though the Qb3 ideas are described as a modern attempt to keep the tension. Neither side has long forcing theory in the main lines.

white_ideas.idea: Develop quickly: Nc3, Nf3, Bf4 with the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain, e3, Bd3, and castle.
4.Bf4 first to prevent ...e5, or 4.Nc3 as the standard, less drawish move.
Qb3 to target b7 (a recent idea), forcing ...Na5 and then Qa4+ so that Black's light-squared bishop goes to d7, inside the pawn chain.
Pressure down the c-file with Rc1 and use the first-move tempo for a small, lasting edge.

black_ideas.idea: Bring the light-squared bishop out with ...Bf5 before playing ...e6, which is the main equalising idea.
Answer Qb3 with ...Na5, attacking the queen and covering b7.
Play ...e6 and ...Bd6, challenge the c-file with ...Rc8, and expand on the queenside with ...a5 and ...b5 for counterplay.
Sit tight: the line offers solid defensive resources with limited winning chances for either side unless White overextends.

typical_structures.structure: Symmetrical d4/d5 structure with e-pawns on e3/e6 (or e-file pawns still to be played) and the c-file open to both sides; rook trades on c1/c8 are common.

Neither side has a c-pawn. A queenside minority attack does not arise from this structure: Black's c-pawn is gone (it recaptured on d5), and the typical queenside play is Qb3 against b7 or ...a5/...b5 by Black.

character.notes: Quiet and symmetrical; 'super solid' (search-result summary), 'the system that takes the fun out of playing the Slav' (Wikipedia). Few forcing lines or sharp tactics; the Qb3 line has some concrete play (Na5, Qa4+). Mostly drawish in practice.

gambit.notes: No pawn is given. The c-pawn exchange (cxd5 cxd5) restores material at once.

soundness.notes: Fully sound for both sides. Wikipedia: gives White minimal advantage beyond the first-move edge. Search snippet: 'in recent years' considered a viable approach for an edge with White (4.Nc3 and Qb3 ideas), but Black has sufficient play (Bf5, Na5).

structure.notes: Symmetrical centre with d4/d5 pawns facing each other and the c-file open; the pawns stay in tension and the centre rarely opens quickly. Could be read as a tense/closed centre with open c-file; sources stress 'static' and 'symmetrical' rather than open or locked.

approach.notes: Standard branch of the Slav against the Queen's Gambit, not a set-up played against everything. Wikipedia says it is primarily a drawing weapon used by top players to neutralise Black's counterplay. Black can avoid it with the Triangle System (2...e6 3...c6). Chess.com: popular at all levels.

level.notes: Chess.com: relatively straightforward to learn, both sides reach balanced positions, popular at all levels as it avoids unnecessary complications. Little forced theory; the difficulty is knowing the piece placement (Bf5 before e6, Na5 against Qb3) and handling symmetrical positions without a clear pawn break.

plan_phrases: dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain

sublines_that_differ.name: Qb3 with Na5 and Qa4+
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 c6 3. Nf3 Nf6 4. cxd5 cxd5 5. Nc3 Nc6 6. Bf4 Bf5 7. Qb3
sublines_that_differ.how: More concrete: queen manoeuvres against b7 and the black bishop, with ...Na5 and Qa4+.

sublines_that_differ.name: 4.Bf4 first
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 c6 3. cxd5 cxd5 4. Bf4
sublines_that_differ.how: Prevents ...e5 lines and keeps a choice of knight development.

description.claim: The Exchange Variation leads to a symmetrical pawn structure, often a quiet, strategic game.
description.note: Symmetrical and static; Wikipedia and the study both describe it that way.
'Drawish' and 'a drawing weapon' appear in the sources.

description.claim: White aims to leverage the first-move advantage for subtle pressure, often through a queenside minority attack.
description.note: The first-move edge is mentioned, but no source describes a minority attack here. Black's c-pawn has gone (cxd5 cxd5), so there is no minority attack against c6; the known White ideas are Bf4, Qb3 against b7 and Rc1.

description.claim: It suits patient, strategic players who enjoy manoeuvring and exploiting small imbalances.
description.note: Chess.com says it is straightforward and popular at all levels; no source frames it as suiting a particular player type.

common_plans.claim: White: execute a queenside minority attack with b4-b5 to create a weakness on Black's c6 pawn.
common_plans.note: Black has no c6 pawn after cxd5 cxd5 (the pawn recaptured on d5). Own understanding (unsourced): this is the Carlsbad-structure plan from the QGD Exchange, not the Slav Exchange.

common_plans.claim: Black: counter the minority attack (...a6 and ...b5) and seek counterplay in the centre or on the kingside.
common_plans.note: There is no minority attack to counter. Black's real queenside play is ...a5/...b5 and ...Rc8, plus ...Na5 against Qb3.

common_plans.claim: Both sides: manoeuvre pieces to control the open c-file and prepare a favourable endgame transition.
common_plans.note: c-file control (Rc1, ...Rc8) and rook trades are typical; 'endgame transition' is the author's framing.

common_plans.claim: White: develop harmoniously and patiently, using the extra tempo to create a small but lasting advantage.
common_plans.note: Matches the 'minimal advantage beyond the first-move edge' description.
